idiom_name: HttpContext.User (ClaimsPrincipal) with AsyncLocal<T> / IHttpContextAccessor for flow beyond the request object
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core makes the request object the container: authentication middleware sets HttpContext.User, a ClaimsPrincipal that assembles every authenticated identity, and application code reads HttpContext.User or has the ClaimsPrincipal bound to a minimal-API parameter, while authorization policies evaluate the same principal. Code that must reach the principal without an HttpContext - an awaited continuation, a service deep in the object graph - reads it through IHttpContextAccessor or a dedicated AsyncLocal<SecurityContext>, whose value follows the asynchronous control flow (the class is documented as ambient data local to an asynchronous flow) but not work started with Task.Run. The classic context class is therefore replaced by ClaimsPrincipal plus the ambient accessor; a hand-written context is justified only when several attributes must travel that ClaimsPrincipal does not naturally carry, and it must not become a second source of truth.
pitfalls: HttpContext must not be captured in a field or held beyond the request; use IHttpContextAccessor or copy the principal when a service needs it later.
AsyncLocal values flow into awaited continuations but not into work started with Task.Run or a fresh thread - that work sees null and must be handed the principal explicitly.
Do not add a second ambient principal (a Thread.CurrentPrincipal-style store) alongside HttpContext.User: two sources of truth for identity drift apart and defeat the pattern.
